newsitem.title: UK: Nigerian crudes adopt new seasonal pattern.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian crudes adopt new seasonal pattern.

text.p: Nigerian crude oil differentials are losing their traditional relationships with each other as changes in buyers' quality demands has created a multi-tiered market, traders say.

And the pattern suggests more than just a seasonal shift in grade preference now that the European market is absorbing a big slice of Nigeria's spot crude cargoes, which would once have travelled to U.S. refineries.
"The traditional relationships have broken up...The light grades used to travel together quite well but that is no longer the case," a trader for a major oil company said.
He added it was difficult now to put lighter grades such as Brass River, Escravos and Bonny Light into one basket and the distillate-rich crudes Forcados and Bonny Medium in another.

"This is what we are seeing now. I don't know if this is a pattern for the future but at the moment it certainly appears as if Bonny Light, Qua Iboe, Brass and Escravos are going one way and Forcados another," another London-based trader active in the West African market said.

Three years ago, differentials for the three crudes known as BBQ -- Bonny Light, Brass River and Qua Iboe -- were all the same. But NNPC changed the price formula to add a quality premium to Brass River over Qua Iboe and Bonny Light, which came to be known as BQ.
NNPC's motive at the time was to obtain a maximum price for its gasoline-rich grades, which include Pennington.

But buyers' demands in recent months and low stock levels of heating oil in Europe and the U.S. have changed, with gas oil grades ruling the roost. In recent trades, Brass River has been shunned in favour of Forcados and Qua Iboe is trading at a discount to BQ.
"Forcados is obviously in good demand and Medium tags along with it," the London-based trader said.
"Bonny Light for similar reasons is more in demand into Europe because of the distillates yield and is doing better than Qua Iboe," he added.

The main reason for the change is that European refiners, seeking to maximise gas oil production to fill up depleted inventories into the northern hemisphere winter, have turned increasingly to West Africa for short-haul crude supplies.
And, given the depressed value of Dated or physical Brent -- against which Nigerian crude is priced -- West African oil is cheap compared with comparable North Sea grades.
Refiners' preference for nearby crudes, given high outright prices in a backwardated market, has meant less West African crude has moved to the Far East and to the U.S., traders say.
Also the economics of taking crude West has not worked for either West African or North Sea crudes in recent months, leaving European customers able to take their pick of West African grades.

"Normally we see a lot of Qua Iboe going to the United States. It does go to Europe as well but the preference is for Bonny Light and not Qua in Europe. I don't know if this situation has arisen because the arbitrage to the U.S. is not working that we have had this differential," the trader said.
"So you have this funny situation at the moment where normally Qua Iboe trades at a premium to BQ, which is not the case at the moment," he said.

"Qua Iboe very rarely goes East. Given that fact and given the preference in Europe, these are the reasons for Escravos and Qua Iboe being at a discount to BQ," he said. "I'm not sure if this is a guide to the future but it is certainly true at the moment."

But the trader also thought the values for Escravos, which has also lost its edge to trade at a discount to BQ, may have now found a floor with U.S. buyers starting to shop around for December barrels.
The rush for Forcados and Bonny Medium has left both grades tight for first decade December with an overhang of lighter grades threatening to weigh on January barrels, traders said.
"You still have lighter grades like Escravos, Qua Iboe, Brass wich have broken up their relationship with BQ and, not surprisingly, there are availabilities of those grades," a trader said.
